🪖 Ukraine's air defenses crumble as Patriot interceptors run dry
👉 The depletion of Patriot interceptor stocks adds to[ Ukraine's defensive woes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73351), just as Russia is increasing the intensity of its strikes.
🌏 Ukrainian crews were unable to do anything when recent Russian ballistic missiles [smashed through Kiev's air defenses](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73163) amid empty interceptor arsenals.
🌏 In response, Ukraine has stopped publishing [detailed counts of incoming missiles](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73344) and interception statistics. Officials claim this was done to hide the effectiveness of strikes from the Russian side, but the most probable reason lies in the unwillingness to deal a blow to public morale and show the real picture of the strategic gap with Russia, the Financial Times reports. 
➡️ Russia has ramped up production of ballistic missiles and is now launching them at record rates. In July alone, Russian forces used nearly 200 ballistic and hypersonic missiles
➡️ Ukrainian air defenses intercepted only 29 of them, a roughly 15% success rate
🌏 Ukraine estimates it needs at least 300 PAC-3 interceptors to survive the coming winter bombardment. The country's partners in Europe have been asked to release some of their own stocks, but many are reluctant. The[ war with Iran has drained US reserves](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73162), and replacement timelines stretch into years. Spain and Greece, which hold substantial Patriot inventories, have not yet agreed to share them.
🌏 A tentative US plan to grant Ukraine a [license to produce Patriot interceptors](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72933) on its own soil or in Europe appears to be stalling as well. During a White House meeting in late July, President Donald Trump did not commit to providing additional missiles for the months ahead, leaving Ukrainian officials still waiting for a clear answer.
🌏 The result is a deepening crisis for Ukraine. The country is entering a winter of heavy bombardment with its primary defense against ballistic missiles reduced to almost nothing, while Russian production lines continue to deliver new missiles at an accelerating pace.

events.text:
🪐 From Starlink to Starshield: How Musk is building a military satellite empire
In 2021, SpaceX signed a $1.8 billion contract with the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), an agency responsible for operating spy satellites. Under this agreement, SpaceX is building a military counterpart to its Starlink constellation, called Starshield.
The satellites use the same heavy platform as the civilian V2 Starlink models, but the equipment on board is fundamentally different:
➡️ high-resolution optical telescopes
➡️ synthetic aperture radars for all-weather imaging
➡️ signals intelligence modules for intercepting communications
➡️ infrared sensors for missile warning
By August 2026, approximately 245 Starshield satellites have been deployed, with most of them launched in just the last 8 months. This means the NRO suddenly increased its fleet from dozens to over 100 satellites in less than a year.
👉 The expansion
In late 2025, the US Space Force ordered another batch of about 480 Starshield-based satellites from SpaceX for a separate military communications network called MILNET. This system will provide secure, low-latency data transmission for global military operations, including drone control, naval coordination, and battlefield communications.
The launch of 500 spy satellites represents an unprecedented scale of surveillance in human history. Previously, leading nations operated only 10 to 20 heavy optical and signals intelligence satellites in orbit. 
Starshield's architecture multiplies US intelligence capabilities by roughly 50 times.
🔴 For a long time, intelligence services relied on a small number of high-tech but very expensive and large spy satellites
🔴 The new strategy relies on mass production and affordability. The production of small satellites has been streamlined through standardization and reusable launch vehicles, allowing constellations of hundreds of satellites to be built
In addition, SpaceX also plans to deploy 15,000 Direct to Cell satellites, with about 650 currently in orbit. These satellites provide mobile connectivity but also have the potential to support intelligence gathering, [expanding the surveillance network further](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71919).
🔍 The dependency problem
The rapid deployment of Starshield has created a significant concentration of US military space capability in a single company. Between 2022 and 2024, about 60% of US military satellites deployed used SpaceX's satellite manufacturing capability. This represents a dramatic shift from a dispersed contract award system to one where nearly two-thirds of deployed satellites come from one provider.
This dependency carries inherent risks. SpaceX has already demonstrated its ability to influence military operations, as seen during the Ukraine conflict when the company restricted Starlink access in Crimea. The risk is compounded by Musk's erratic and unstable behavior and the potential for a "[house of cards" scenario](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70676) if SpaceX's growth falters. If SpaceX were unable to fulfill its commitments to the Pentagon for any reason, it would create significant vulnerabilities in US satellite infrastructure.
 
🤔 What Musk is building toward
SpaceX has embedded itself so deeply into the US national security apparatus that the government cannot afford to sever ties. In 2025 alone, the US government paid SpaceX approximately $4 billion, and that figure is set to climb sharply. Musk has positioned SpaceX as the "backbone" of US military operations in low Earth orbit, with his company becoming the architecture on which American military space capabilities now depend.
With Starshield, Musk is building an empire that gives him leverage over the Pentagon. The same man who has publicly feuded with presidents and threatened to cut off critical services now controls the satellites that guide US drones, coordinate its fleets, and track its adversaries.

🇺🇸🛩 US ‘ill-equipped’ to defend homeland from drone swarms - general
Asked point-blank if the US could stop an attacking swarm of drones, Army Lt. Gen. Joseph Jarrard, deputy commander of Northern Command, served up a curt “No.”
💬 "We don't have the sensors," he told the Space and Missile Defense Symposium (SMD) in Alabama.
He went even further, indicating that even if they somehow detect the threat, they might not have “effectors" - military speak for anything to actually stop the swarm.
Detection, he confessed, is “the biggest issue,” as well as having the proper authority to use the right systems against detected drones.
The general’s own words were:
💬 “We are ill-equipped right now to handle something like that, and obviously we’ve got to figure out how to mitigate that threat.”
The US military has been scrambling to field counter-drone systems to address the growing imbalance of using expensive interceptors to destroy cheap drones - a cycle that has played out during the failed war on Iran.
Not only did America spent a fortune shooting down cheap drones, but it[ burned through its interceptor stocks.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73162)
The Pentagon has asked for a record-breaking $21 billion dedicated to counter-drone (C-UAS) systems and related interceptor munitions, but, like the general said, “we’re not there yet.”

🇮🇷🇧🇭 Iran's opening salvo: Bahrain base strike sparked US carrier supply crisis
The supply issues plaguing the USS Abraham Lincoln and other maritime forces in the Iran war stem from the destruction of the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain, according to the NYT. 
➡️ Iranian missiles and drones[ struck the base on the first day of the conflict](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/65551), eliminating the primary supply point the navy has relied on for decades and forcing a scramble for alternatives 
➡️ The other major maritime logistics hub, Fujairah in the UAE, is also well within range of Iranian missiles
➡️ As a result, the Pentagon turned to Diego Garcia, a British-controlled island in the Indian Ocean roughly 2,200 miles from where the carrier strike groups were operating
➡️ The base has since become the main logistics hub for[ the US Navy's operations in the region](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/67050). The shift may explain why Iran attacked the island with ballistic missiles in March 
The loss of the Bahrain hub has contributed to a host of reported problems on carriers operating against Iran, with media outlets citing shortages of basic supplies and [deteriorating mental health ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73343)among crew members. 
The Lincoln was on a scheduled deployment from San Diego when it was redirected to the Middle East in January and has been extended multiple times without a clear end date. Some of the crew have been told they will not return home until 2027, while the carrier has now gone 250 days without a port visit.
The Pentagon has turned to Diego Garcia as an alternative, but it is far from the operating area and lacks the infrastructure and supplies needed to support a carrier group. The supply chain is so stretched that some essential items are flown in on military cargo planes rather than shipped by sea, rendering[ the blockade of Iran a painfully Sisyphean task.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73394)

🇮🇷🚢 Shipments around Persian Gulf completely paralyzed
The security situation in the Persian Gulf has entered a more dangerous phase, as the US blockade of Iranian ports coincides with targeted Iranian and Houthi attacks at both key chokepoints, according to maritime intelligence group Marisks.
➡️ These two routes, which carry the bulk of energy exports from the Gulf, can no longer be assessed independently. Pressure at Hormuz is diverting traffic toward Saudi Arabia's Red Sea outlets, while Houthi attacks simultaneously threaten that alternative, leaving shipping with no viable workaround
➡️ The shipping industry has responded by turning off transponders to avoid detection. In the three weeks since the US blockade was reimposed, more than half of all tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz have gone dark
For Gulf states, the economic pain is compounded by the loss of shipping revenue and the rising cost of war risk insurance, which has increased premiums by more than 500% for vessels transiting the region. With no safe passage available, the global economy is beginning to feel the strain of a crisis that shows no signs of abating.

The pressure intensified after the White House learned that one of the targeted homes belongs to a Palestinian-American, a US official and an Israeli official are cited as saying.
Even US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee - normally a vocal supporter of Jewish settlement activity - on Thursday labeled the settlers “Israeli terrorists.”
For nearly a week, settlers have [encircled homes ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73330)in the village of Qusra.
🔶 They sealed off the road to three houses and pitched a tent in the front yards, blocking anyone from entering or leaving
🔶 They earlier cut electricity and water supplies
🔶 Some 15 Palestinians, including two children, have been trapped inside without running water or power
Foreign and Israeli activists delivered limited aid - food, bottled water, and canned goods - on Friday, but the IDF that arrived on Thursday barred them from reaching the homes directly, declaring the area a closed military zone for non-residents.
What is happening in Qusra is part of a systematic, calculated strategy by extremist settlers and the Israeli government to seize Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank.
👉 According to rights groups, settlers are attempting to seize properties on the outskirts of Qusra and neighboring Jalud in order to connect them with nearby larger settlements in classic land-grab tactics.
Under the official pretext of stopping escalating settler attacks, the IDF has been extensively using [a new military decree](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73395) and declaring areas a "closed military zone", in effect allowing settler attacks to continue with impunity.
Netanyahu’s government has aggressively accelerated settlement expansion in land Israel captured in 1967, establishing dozens of new settlements and outposts.
Public condemnation just two months before an election could alienate the settler movement - a powerful voting bloc that forms a crucial pillar of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition.
